h1: The 6 Best Ultrawide Monitor Arms of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Ultrawide Monitor Arms: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 ultrawide monitor arms scored on weight rating, screen width, spring type and warranty, from WALI to Ergotron and Secretlab.
summary: The ARES WING is the best ultrawide arm for most people: a gas spring that carries up to 44 lbs, fits screens from 17 to 49 inches, and explicitly names the Samsung Odyssey G9. The HUANUO TitanLift is the sturdier alternative with a 5-year warranty. The Secretlab Magnus handles the widest panels, up to 57 inches, and the WALI is the budget pick for 33 lb screens.
intro: Ultrawide monitors punish ordinary arms in a way flat panels never do. The weight sits far from the pole, so the arm has to resist torque, not just load. A mount that holds a 27-inch screen perfectly can droop on a 34-inch curved panel with the same listed weight, because the center of mass sits out in front of the clamp. Nearly every complaint about sagging ultrawides comes from this.

So we ranked arms by capacity for wide, curved panels first: weight rating, maximum screen width and the type of spring. We reviewed spec sheets and owner feedback for six arms, from a budget WALI to the 57-inch-rated Secretlab, and scored each on the Primea framework. Warranty length counted too, since an arm under constant torque is only as good as the guarantee behind it.

products.name: ARES WING Ultrawide Monitor Desk Arm
products.verdict: A 44 lb gas-spring arm built around super-ultrawide panels like the Odyssey G9.
products.description:
The ARES WING uses an industrial gas spring, fits screens from 17 to 49 inches and carries up to 44 lbs. The listing names the Samsung Odyssey G9 and LG super-ultrawides as compatible, which is rare: most arms only claim a generic 49-inch rating.

It leads because capacity and clarity both land. Against the WALI, you double the weight headroom from 33 to 44 lbs for a modest increase in price, which matters when a 49-inch panel is heavy. Against the Ergotron HX at 42 lbs, you gain 2 lbs and a lower price bracket, though you give up Ergotron's 10-year warranty.

Buy it for a 49-inch super-ultrawide that other arms may not carry. The caveat is the 3-year warranty, the shortest of the heavy-duty options here, and it uses a C-clamp or grommet mount that needs a sturdy desk edge.
products.idealFor: Owners of 49-inch super-ultrawides such as the Odyssey G9.
products.skipIf: You want the longest warranty or the lowest cost.

products.name: HUANUO TitanLift Heavy Duty Monitor Arm
products.verdict: Reinforced aluminum that resists curved-panel torque, with a 5-year warranty.
products.description:
The TitanLift fits screens up to 49 inches at up to 44 lbs, using reinforced aluminum designed for the twisting force of curved panels. The maker says the arm is 20 percent thicker and the base 30 percent wider than its standard model, and rates it for 50,000 movement cycles.

It ranks second behind the ARES WING because the listing does not name a specific super-ultrawide, though the capacity is identical at 44 lbs. Where it pulls ahead is the 5-year warranty and the dual C-clamp mount, which spreads load across the desk edge. Against the WALI, you gain 11 lbs of capacity and a longer guarantee.

Buy it if you want reinforcement against sag over the long term. The caveat is that the dual clamp needs more desk edge clearance than a single clamp.
cons: Dual clamp needs more edge space
products.idealFor: Long-term owners of heavy curved ultrawides who value the warranty.
products.skipIf: Your desk edge is too thin or too cluttered for a dual clamp.

products.name: Secretlab Magnus Monitor Arm (Heavy Duty Edition)
products.verdict: Rated up to 57 inches, the widest capacity in this ranking.
products.description:
The Magnus is rated up to 57 inches, the widest in this ranking, with an 18 to 35 lb capacity and a premium tensile spring made for curved-panel torque. It also includes magnetic cable management, and it is designed specifically for ultrawide gaming monitors.

It ranks third because the 35 lb ceiling is lower than the ARES and HUANUO at 44 lbs. Width and weight are separate limits, and a heavy 49-inch panel may fit the Magnus by size yet exceed its load. Against the Ergotron HX, which carries up to 42 lbs, the Magnus is the better choice only if screen width is the constraint.

Buy it for a 57-inch-class monitor that is not too heavy. The caveat is the 18 lb minimum: a lighter panel will not balance the spring, and the $200 to $500 bracket is steep.
products.idealFor: Gamers with very wide panels that sit between 18 and 35 lbs.
products.skipIf: Your monitor is lighter than 18 lbs or heavier than 35 lbs.

products.name: WALI Heavy Duty Single Monitor Arm
products.verdict: A 33 lb aviation-grade aluminum arm for 17 to 49 inch screens, at the lowest price.
products.description:
The WALI uses aviation-grade aluminum, fits 17 to 49 inch screens up to 33 lbs, and adds gas spring height adjustment with 360 degree rotation. A zero-drift design aims to keep the screen where you set it, and a 3-year warranty comes with the C-clamp or grommet mount.

It ranks fourth because the 33 lb limit leaves less margin than the 44 lb ARES or HUANUO. Many 34-inch ultrawides weigh under that, which makes the WALI a sensible fit, but a 49-inch panel can crowd the rating. The price bracket of $25 to $50 makes it a bargain against the Secretlab at $200 to $500.

Buy it for a standard 34-inch ultrawide on a budget. The caveat is that headroom shrinks fast on a super-ultrawide.
products.idealFor: Owners of 34-inch ultrawides who want a capable arm for little spend.

products.name: Ergotron HX Premium Heavy Duty Monitor Arm
products.verdict: A 20 to 42 lb Ergotron with a 10-year warranty for flat or slightly curved 49-inch screens.
products.description:
The Ergotron HX is rated for 20 to 42 lbs, supports flat or slightly curved screens up to 49 inches, offers an 11.5-inch lift with 360 degree rotation, and fits VESA 200x200mm. It carries a 10-year warranty.

It ranks fifth because it costs the most among the 49-inch-capable arms at $200 to $500, yet its 42 lb ceiling sits below the 44 lbs of the ARES and HUANUO. The listing also says slightly curved, not fully curved, so a strongly curved 49-inch panel is the wrong fit. What you buy is Ergotron's long warranty and build reputation.

Buy it if a decade of coverage matters and your screen is flat or gently curved. The caveat is the 20 lb minimum, which lighter monitors will not satisfy.

keySpecs.label: Screen fit
keySpecs.value: Up to 49 inches, flat or slightly curved

products.idealFor: Buyers who want a decade of coverage on a flat or gently curved 49-inch screen.
products.skipIf: Your panel is strongly curved or lighter than 20 lbs.

products.name: Ergotron LX Monitor Arm
products.verdict: The proven Ergotron arm, rated up to 34 inches, not for super-ultrawides.
products.description:
The Ergotron LX is rated for 7 to 25 lbs and screens up to 34 inches, flat or curved ultrawide. It offers a 13-inch lift, 360 degree rotation, 75 degrees of tilt and fits VESA 75x75 or 100x100mm, with a 10-year warranty, the longest in this list.

It ranks last because it is not rated for 49-inch super-ultrawides, and a 25 lb ceiling is the lowest here. For a 34-inch ultrawide, though, it is a superb fit, and it costs less than the HX at $100 to $200. Against the WALI, you get a longer warranty and a trusted build, but less weight capacity.

Buy it for a standard 34-inch ultrawide. The caveat is exactly the size limit: do not stretch it to a 49-inch panel.
products.idealFor: Owners of a standard 34-inch ultrawide who want a decade of coverage.

methodology.description: Ultrawides load an arm with torque, so we ranked the maximum load, from 25 to 44 lbs, ahead of every other spec.

methodology.description: Rated screen sizes from 34 to 57 inches decide which panels fit, so we matched each arm to realistic ultrawide formats.

methodology.title: Spring and mechanism
methodology.description: Gas springs, tensile springs and reinforced frames differ in how they resist droop on a curved panel.

methodology.title: Warranty

whatMatters.detail: A 49-inch super-ultrawide can weigh far more than a 27-inch flat screen. Find your monitor's weight without the stand in its manual, then check it sits inside the arm's rated range. Remember arms like the Ergotron HX and Secretlab Magnus also set a minimum load for the spring to balance.

Rated width is how big a panel the arm geometry supports. The Ergotron LX stops at 34 inches, most others go to 49, and the Secretlab reaches 57. A panel wider than the rating can overload the pivot even if the weight is acceptable. Check the width line in the title.

Gas springs and tensile springs counter the weight with a stored force. A spring tuned for a heavy curved panel holds position without creeping. Look for words like industrial gas spring or tensile spring, and note whether the listing adjusts tension with a screw.

A curved ultrawide pulls forward and down on the arm. Reinforced aluminum and wider bases, as on the HUANUO TitanLift, resist that twist. Treat any listing that says slightly curved, like the Ergotron HX, as unsuitable for a deeply curved 49-inch screen.

Constant torque wears pivots and springs, so a long warranty is worth real money. Ergotron offers 10 years, HUANUO 5 years and several others 3 years. Read the warranty line in the bullets, and check whether it covers the spring specifically.

faq.q: Will the ARES WING hold a Samsung Odyssey G9?
faq.a: The listing names the Odyssey G9 and LG super-ultrawides as compatible, with a 49-inch fit and a 44 lb rating. Weigh your specific unit without its stand first, and confirm it sits inside that load range before mounting.

faq.q: What mistake do people make with ultrawide arms?
faq.a: They match the weight rating and ignore panel width and curve. The Ergotron LX is excellent at 34 inches but not rated for a 49-inch screen, and the Ergotron HX is for flat or slightly curved panels only.

faq.q: Is the Secretlab Magnus worth over the HUANUO TitanLift?
faq.a: Only if your screen exceeds 49 inches. The Secretlab is rated to 57 inches but carries 35 lbs against the TitanLift's 44, and it sits in the $200 to $500 bracket. For most 49-inch monitors, the HUANUO is the stronger buy.

faq.q: How do I set up a clamp mount safely?
faq.a: Check the desk edge thickness against the clamp range, tighten gradually and test with the monitor attached before removing support. A grommet mount through a hole can be steadier on thin desks. The HUANUO's dual clamp needs extra edge clearance.

faq.q: How often should I retension the spring?
faq.a: Retension when the screen drifts, which is most often in the first months and after changing monitors. The ARES WING and WALI use gas springs with adjustment, while the Secretlab uses a tensile spring that may need a tool.

faq.q: Can a single arm hold a 49-inch monitor safely?
faq.a: Yes, if the arm is rated for it. The ARES WING, HUANUO TitanLift and Ergotron HX list 49-inch ratings, but check your monitor's weight against 44, 44 and 42 lbs respectively, and the VESA pattern against the arm's plate.

finalTake: For most ultrawide owners the ARES WING is the arm to buy: a 44 lb gas spring, a 49-inch rating and a named Odyssey G9 fit. If you want a reinforced build and a 5-year warranty, the HUANUO TitanLift is the sturdier alternative. The Secretlab Magnus is for panels up to 57 inches, and the WALI is the budget pick for a 34-inch ultrawide.
